articles.headline: Rupee Co-operative Bank replay: the signal was an evidence boundary, not a clean warning
articles.dek: This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Rupee Co-operative Bank’s record shows why a balance-sheet screen must separate a filing-period signal, a market-price signal, and an absence of scoreable evidence.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Similar balance-sheet mechanisms do not imply the same outcome.* Rupee Co-operative Bank defaulted on 2022-09-22. The supplied record does not identify a balance sheet that should have felt stress first through a usable public signal. Its central lesson is narrower, but important: an unscoreable record is an evidence boundary, not a benign result.

That conclusion is not a retrospective claim that the institution was healthy before the event. It is also not a claim that a model detected what the available inputs did not show. A filing-period signal depends on published, scoreable institutional disclosures. A market-price signal depends on an observable market repricing measure. A model derivation is an output constructed from its inputs and assumptions. These are different evidentiary objects, and none can be substituted for another when the record is missing.

A Failure Radar tier is a published rule over published components, not a solvency verdict, a failure prediction, or **not a credit rating**. Rupee Co-operative Bank is a useful hard case precisely because a failed institution need not leave a neat, timely trail for every public screen.

## The record before the event

The replay records Rupee Co-operative Bank as an urban co-operative bank, with the event date of 2022-09-22. Fraud masking is marked false. That means this case is not tagged as one in which later-discovered falsification made apparently compliant filings misleading. It does not establish capital strength, asset quality, liquidity, funding resilience, or prior safety.

The institution-specific PCA record contains no first action-zone observation and no lead time. The funding record is explicitly unscoreable, with no first signal and no lead time. The dossier supplies no historical filing as-of date for the institution. That date cannot be inferred from the default date, the publication date, or a later board timestamp.

The relevant record is therefore the [Rupee Co-operative Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/rupee-co-operative-bank/), not a current institutional dossier. The Failure Radar board is dated 2026-09-01 and its market layer is dated 2026-08-11. Those dates describe later analytical material, not information demonstrably available before Rupee Co-operative Bank’s event.

## What the lenses saw

Read literally, neither named balance-sheet lens supplies a usable lead in this case. The PCA lens does not show a first action-zone breach. The funding lens cannot operate without a scoreable liability series. Neither result says that pressure was absent. It says the supplied replay cannot establish that either lens observed it first.

That distinction becomes sharper under the historical construction label: `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`. The record is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. Where an explicit publication clock is absent, availability is proxied by period end plus 60 days. The dossier also states that lead times are optimistic. A period-end proxy may impose a conservative delay convention, but it still does not prove the actual information set available to a lender, depositor, investor, or supervisor at that time.

The broader replay gives context but cannot fill this institution’s gaps. Across failed institutions, the PCA summary reports 15 cases, with 5 entering the action zone first and a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary also reports 15 failed institutions, but only 10 have liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first in 4, with a median lead of 38 months. Those are cohort descriptions, not proof that Rupee Co-operative Bank travelled either path. The [validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation) preserves those limits.

## Why the warning mattered

The warning here was epistemic. A desk seeking to rank balance-sheet stress needed evidence on supervisory-threshold inputs or liabilities, with a credible availability date. The replay does not provide a scoreable funding series and does not provide a first PCA action-zone observation. The proper result is an unresolved institution-specific record.

That matters because absence is easily misread. “No signal” can mean that a threshold did not fire on available inputs. “No score” can mean that the needed inputs were unavailable or unusable. “No market-price signal” would mean something else again: that a market-based measure was absent, unavailable, or did not cross its own rule. These states cannot honestly be collapsed into “no risk.”

The methodology says components are replayed independently on a 48-institution construction-PIT record and fused only for presentation. It also says the conformal alarm is diagnostic, with no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Those constraints are not footnotes. They prevent a model derivation from being presented as a contemporaneous observation.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any stronger thesis: this replay may be too incomplete to say which balance sheet would have felt stress first, or whether either disclosed lens would have given a useful warning before the event. Pressure may have emerged outside the captured series, moved more quickly than the filing proxy, or remained outside the supplied public record.

The validation statistics reinforce caution. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a CI95 range of 0.338 to 1.0. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and failed that gate. On the same held-out rows, the heuristic AUC is 0.799.

Those figures do not establish that the screen is useless. They do establish that historical discrimination is uncertain and that construction-PIT diagnostics cannot be promoted into a tradable or decision-ready backtest. The counter-case therefore defeats any assertion that Rupee Co-operative Bank was cleanly flagged. It does not defeat the narrower thesis that the honest output is a documented blind spot rather than reassurance.

## What today's board shares

Today’s board is a separate comparison, not historical evidence about this institution. As of 2026-09-01, it reports 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with a score of 74.9 and a dossier as of 2025-03-31 that is 18 months old. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8, as of 2026-03-31 and 6 months old. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow at 66.0, as of 2025-09-30 and 12 months old, with market distance-to-default of 1.927 and the `market_dd_below_2` signal.

These are current screen states, not forecasts. The board excludes 21 stale institutions, and nothing older than 24 months is presented as current. Its market layer uses daily auto-adjusted Yahoo Finance closes through 2026-08-11, documented in the [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets). An absent institution is not thereby green; Rupee Co-operative Bank’s replay shows why.

## The next falsifiable test

This account can be disproved with a genuinely bitemporal, pre-event public record. It would need dated filings or disclosures, a verified publication clock, and scoreable PCA or liability-series inputs. If that record showed a timely action-zone breach or funding signal, the replay should identify the first lens and its lead time.

If it instead showed neither signal before the event despite verified timely availability, the claim that the key warning was an evidence boundary would be weakened. Either result would be more informative than retrospective reconstruction from later dates. Until then, the missing data must remain visible rather than being converted into a signal.

## Follow the pressure chain

For a risk committee, the sequence is procedural: establish the filing or publication date; test whether supervisory-threshold inputs are scoreable; test whether liability disclosures exist; then separate any market repricing observation from the filing-based evidence. A missing link stops the inference chain. It does not complete it.

LiquiLens addresses **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. Seiche addresses **system dollar-funding capacity**, as described in the [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview). Undertow addresses **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**, as shown on the [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json). The questions can be related, but system funding, an institution balance sheet, and executable market exit are not interchangeable measurements.

## Sources, method, and limits

The core materials are the [Rupee Co-operative Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/rupee-co-operative-bank/), the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), the [historical validation file](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), and the [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets). Additional desk material is available through [LiquiLens research](https://liquilens.in/research/) and the [investigations archive](https://liquilens.in/investigations/).

This is a public-disclosure replay with period-end proxy construction timing, not a validated backtest or a real-money test. Lead times are optimistic. Fraud-masked filings can appear compliant to threshold engines; this case is not fraud-masked, but that general limitation remains. **This is not investment advice.**

articles.headline: Before the event: what Sri Guru Raghavendra Sahakara Bank's filings did and did not reveal
articles.dek: A construction-PIT replay of Sri Guru Raghavendra Sahakara Bank: the first published regulatory or funding signal, the disclosure clock, the miss, and the boundary that survives into today's screen.
articles.body_markdown:
Nothing in today's Failure Radar evidence cleared the bar for a fresh institution story. This is therefore a historical replay, **not current news and not a forecast**. It opens the public Sri Guru Raghavendra Sahakara Bank record because a quiet daily tape is better used to examine what an early-warning system could actually have known than to manufacture a new alarm.

The recorded outcome date is **2020-01-10**. LiquiLens's reconstruction asks two narrower questions. Did the disclosed ratios enter a published regulatory action zone? Did the disclosed liability structure enter a funding-fragility band? It does not ask whether a modern model, armed with later revisions and hindsight, can draw a persuasive line through the event.

## The record before the event

The first regulatory action-zone row is dated **not observed**, with a conservative knowledge-time proxy of **not available**. Its status is **no action-zone entry in the record**, its breached fields are **none published**, and its recorded lead is **unavailable months**.

The funding replay is independently scoreable: **True**. Its first signal is dated **not observed**, with knowledge-time proxy **not available**, index **unavailable**, band **not observed**, flags **none published**, and lead **unavailable months**.

Those two rows are allowed to disagree. Regulatory thresholds look for capital and asset-quality boundaries. Funding fragility looks for liability dependence and rollover exposure. One can fire while the other stays silent because they describe different failure physics.

## What the lenses saw

The [public replay page](https://liquilens.in/replay/sri-guru-raghavendra-sahakara-bank/) preserves the observed entries and misses side by side. The regulatory lens reports the institution against the framework's own tripwires. The funding lens requires liability disclosures and abstains when a usable series is absent. The hazard model excludes fraud-masked failures from fitting because fabricated disclosures carry no honest deterioration signal.

Across the full India record, the regulatory replay summary contains **15** failed institutions and **5** first action-zone entries, with a median recorded lead of **41 months**. The funding replay contains **10** institutions with liability disclosures and **4** first funding signals.

Those are diagnostic counts, not a validated backtest. The dossiers use explicit publication time when it exists and otherwise a conservative period-end-plus-filing-lag proxy. The source record says that the missing complete revision archive can make reconstructed lead times optimistic.

## Why the warning mattered

An early warning matters only if it names a mechanism and leaves time to test it. An action-zone breach says capital or asset quality crossed a supervisory boundary. A funding flag says the liability structure may be exposed to rollover or withdrawal. Neither statement proves the eventual outcome; both can tell a risk team what evidence to demand next.

For Sri Guru Raghavendra Sahakara Bank, the useful question is which lens spoke first and which stayed silent. The answer above is more valuable than a blended retrospective score because it preserves responsibility. A ratio model should not take credit for a funding signal, and a funding model should not claim to have seen fabricated assets.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case is the historical construction itself. A period-end metric is not necessarily what a decision-maker saw on that date. Later amendments may overwrite the original. A fixed filing-lag proxy is conservative about immediate availability but cannot reconstruct every revision. That makes this a mechanism diagnostic, not proof of live foresight.

The record's fraud-masked flag for this case is **True**. If true, honest-looking published ratios can be a false negative for any disclosure-based engine. If false, the absence of a signal can still be a real miss. LiquiLens keeps both categories visible because removing them would turn research into marketing.

## What today's board shares

Today's board contains **0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green** rows. That is not evidence that any current institution is “the next Sri Guru Raghavendra Sahakara Bank.” No similarity model is asserted here. The legitimate connection is methodological: current filings, market prices, regulatory distance and funding coverage still arrive on different clocks and can still disagree.

The board also excludes **21** stale dossiers from current presentation. That abstention is part of the signal. An institution missing from the current table is not thereby safe; it may simply lack a fresh vetted record.

## The next falsifiable test

For a current name, record the filing period, knowledge-time proxy and market date before reading the tier. Then ask whether a newer filing confirms the same asset-quality, capital or funding direction. If it reverses, the old screen should fall. If a dark funding lens becomes observable, grade whether it confirms or contradicts the tier. If the model cannot state what would change its mind, the historical lesson has not been learned.

## Follow the pressure chain

[Seiche](https://seiche.info/articles/) asks whether system funding capacity is tightening. [LiquiLens](https://liquilens.in/articles/) asks which institution balance sheet would transmit that pressure. [Undertow](https://liquilens-undertow.com/articles/) asks whether the risk can be exited in traded markets. The three layers may disagree, and that disagreement is often the finding.

Readers who need the rule tested on their own counterparties can use the [six-week proof pilot](https://liquilens.in/pilot/). The public replay, including this case's misses and voids, stays open.

articles.headline: Religare Finvest’s funding signal was early—not a clean prediction of failure
articles.dek: A historical replay places a Watch-band funding reading before Religare Finvest’s default. The narrower lesson is that liability strain can reveal vulnerability before formal thresholds do, while fraud can make disclosure-based screens falsely reassuring.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It is not investment advice, and its risk tier is not a credit rating or a prediction of failure. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome.*

Religare Finvest offers a bounded answer to the desk question of which balance sheet should feel stress first. In this replay, the liability-facing funding lens turned before the recorded default; the PCA record did not show an earlier action-zone entry. That is a filing-period signal, not proof that the market had repriced the institution, and not a model-derived probability that failure would occur.

The distinction is decisive. A filing can reveal a configuration that deserves investigation. A market-price measure can register investors’ repricing of risk. A model can transform specified inputs into a score or tier. None of those things, separately or together, establishes causation—especially where the institution is fraud-masked.

## The record before the event

Religare Finvest is classified as an NBFC. Its recorded default date is **2018-01-18**. The funding lens was scoreable and first registered a Watch-band signal for the period ended **2016-03-31**, at an index of **44.3**. Its knowledge-time proxy is **2016-05-30**, producing a replay lead of **19 months**.

The PCA record has no first action zone and no PCA lead time. That absence does not mean the institution was safe. It says only that this reconstruction does not identify a PCA action-zone signal preceding the event. Conversely, the funding reading does not mean default was inevitable. It identified a disclosed liability-side configuration under the lens’s rules; it did not disclose the event’s full cause.

The Watch observation carried no listed flags. That is not an inconsistency to explain away. A composite or index can identify a vulnerable configuration without naming a single decisive fact, and an unflagged disclosure record can be incomplete or misleading. Religare Finvest’s fraud-masked designation is therefore central, not a footnote: institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine. The forensic screen owns that limitation.

The underlying [Religare Finvest replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/religare-finvest/) should be read as a reconstruction of what a specified public-disclosure process could have surfaced, not as a retrospective claim of certainty.

## What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a Watch-band condition; the PCA lens did not record an action-zone entry first. The most defensible interpretation is narrow: liability-facing information may become concerning before public supervisory tripwires are visible in the available record.

Across the funding summary, **15** failed institutions are included, while **10** had liability disclosures usable by that lens. The funding signal fired first for **4**, with a median lead of **38 months**. This is not a claim about all lenders. It is a disclosure-limited result: the lens cannot see institutions that do not publish a usable liability series.

The PCA summary also covers **15** failed institutions. It records **5** entering an action zone first, with a median lead of **41 months**. The broader India diagnostic covers **48** institutions across two decades and reports that **88.9%** of non-fraud failures were flagged, with a median lead of **21.5 months**. These figures describe a construction-PIT diagnostic, not investable performance.

The [validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), and [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) preserve the relevant eligibility limits. The India record is `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`, is not validated-backtest eligible, is not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract.

## Why the warning mattered

The plausible mechanism is balance-sheet pressure, not prophecy. If funding becomes less resilient, refinancing flexibility can narrow. That can force defensive liquidity management, reduce room to absorb losses, and weaken confidence among creditors or counterparties. Assets may be slower-moving or harder to monetize than liabilities are to renew, making the sequence economically important.

But this is a mechanism for inquiry, not a causal finding about Religare Finvest. The filing-period Watch signal preceded the event. It did not show that funding stress caused it. Nor did it show what the market believed at that point: the dossier provides no Religare-specific market-price signal for that historical date.

A model derivation adds a further layer of distance. The board’s published tier is a rule over published components, while PD levels are corpus-fitted and prior-corrected to a population base rate of approximately **0.25%** per year. That is not the same as an observed market price. Likewise, Merton PD is described as a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. The right response to a funding alert is to examine maturity dependence, liquidity retention, funding composition, and disclosure integrity—not to declare failure forecast.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any stronger thesis. This is a fraud-masked, single-institution replay in which a Watch reading preceded default by **19 months**. That sequence may be hindsight-rich rather than actionable. It does not demonstrate that the signal separated Religare Finvest from institutions that survived, that it was known to all market participants on the proxy date, or that it added value beyond other disclosed measures.

The aggregate model diagnostics are also too fragile for promotion. The hazard panel contains **205** rows, **9** events, and **27** institutions; **179** censored or unusable rows were excluded. Leave-one-institution-out row AUC is **0.752**, with a confidence interval of **0.338** to **1.0**. The heuristic AUC is **0.799** on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is **0.645**, below the **0.65** gate, and remains diagnostic only.

Fraud is more than an error bar. If reported inputs fail to describe the condition of the institution, a threshold engine may appear calm for reasons unrelated to actual resilience. The steel-manned conclusion is therefore that funding may have exposed a relevant vulnerability, but has not earned authority to predict default.

## What today's board shares

The current board is dated **2026-08-30**. It shows **0** red, **1** orange, **3** yellow, and **15** green institutions, and excludes **21** stale cases. An absent institution is not evidence of calm: institutions without fresh vetted public dossiers are absent by design.

Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with a filing as of **2025-03-31** that is **17 months** old. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, as of **2025-09-30** and **11 months** old, with market distance-to-default of **1.927** and a `market_dd_below_2` signal. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow as of **2026-03-31**, **5 months** old.

These are current board classifications over published components, not ratings. Market distance-to-default below **1** can produce orange; below **2** can produce yellow. That is a market-price signal, whereas reported levels and deterioration are filing-period signals. The tier that combines them is a model derivation under a published rule. It cannot repair stale data, missing disclosures, or fraud risk.

## The next falsifiable test

The thesis should fail if prospectively timestamped, original filings show that early funding Watch signals add no useful warning after disclosure quality and other published measures are considered. It should also fail if comparable funding configurations repeatedly refinance without deterioration and the screen cannot distinguish those cases from eventual stress.

A credible test requires exact publication timestamps, original rather than amended disclosures, predefined rules, and outcomes observed after the signal. The present availability basis uses an explicit publication clock when present; otherwise it uses period end plus **60 days**. The resulting lead times are optimistic. Until a bitemporal archive exists, the alert should trigger work rather than a conclusion.

## Follow the pressure chain

Follow disclosed liabilities to refinancing flexibility, liquidity retention, loss absorption, confidence, and the reliability of the disclosure record itself. Do not reverse that logic: no signal does not establish that every link is sound.

LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity**; its current editorial read is guarded, led by modelled or slow-moving structure while current market plumbing has not broadly confirmed it. Undertow covers **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**; its coverage is partial across several segments. These are separate risk layers, not substitutes. The [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) and [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) should not be used to infer institution-level calm.

## Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the [Religare replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/religare-finvest/), the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), the [validation feed](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), the [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets), and [LiquiLens research](https://liquilens.in/research/). The historical signal date, proxy availability date, event date, board date, and market-layer date are different clocks and must not be merged.

The construction is period-end proxied; lead times are optimistic; the bitemporal contract is absent; and fraud can mask a failing institution from threshold logic. Missing data, stale dossiers, and unavailable system context are not evidence of stability.

articles.headline: IL&FS replay: the funding signal arrived before the threshold lenses named a break
articles.dek: IL&FS’s disclosed funding lens reached watch well before default, while the public action-zone replay recorded no first entry. That sequence is a historical prompt for diligence, not proof of foresight or a forecast.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is not current news and not a forecast. It is a historical replay of IL&FS, whose default date was 2018-08-28. Similar balance-sheet mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

The narrow, contestable thesis is that IL&FS should have felt stress first through disclosed funding conditions rather than through the public-disclosure replay of regulatory action-zone thresholds. It does not follow that the funding lens detected every cause of the event, or that it could have supplied an investable warning. IL&FS is fraud-masked, which is precisely why a seemingly orderly filing record cannot settle the question.

The key distinction is between a filing-period signal, a market-price signal, and a model derivation. The funding observation is tied to a reporting period and a publication-time proxy. Market distance-to-default is a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. A score, tier, lead time, or hazard statistic is a model output built from those inputs; it is not a contemporaneous fact about the institution. That separation is the difference between a useful replay and retrospective certainty.

## The record before the event

IL&FS’s first recorded funding signal was a watch reading of 45.4 for the period ended 2015-03-31. The associated knowledge-time proxy was 2015-05-30. Default followed on 2018-08-28, giving the funding lens a recorded lead of 38 months. The PCA replay has no first action-zone entry and no lead time.

Those dates need their clocks attached. The replay is labelled `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`. When an explicit publication clock is unavailable, it uses period end plus 60 days. Lead times are therefore optimistic. The work has no bitemporal input contract, is not validated-backtest eligible, and is not real-money eligible. The limitation is especially severe here. A fraud-masked institution may look compliant to any threshold engine if the underlying filings were later shown to be falsified. The forensic screen owns that problem; mechanical filing thresholds do not solve it. Missing evidence cannot be translated into calm, and a clean-looking ratio history cannot prove that the balance sheet was clean. Readers can inspect the [IL&FS replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/ilfs/) and the wider [replay archive](https://liquilens.in/replay/).

## What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a watch signal first. IL&FS was scoreable because it disclosed a liability series. Its initial observation had no listed flags, yet the index was 45.4 at the stated period end. The PCA lens supplied no action-zone sequence to compare with that signal.

This ordering is consistent with a liability-first pressure path, but it does not prove one. The funding lens sees only institutions with liability disclosures. In the historical summary, 15 institutions failed, 10 had liability disclosures, and the funding signal fired first for 4; its median lead was 38 months. The PCA or SAF public-disclosure replay also covers 15 failed institutions, with 5 entering an action zone first and a median lead of 41 months. ## Why the warning mattered

A funding warning matters as a balance-sheet question, not because an index causes a default. An institution can hold assets that are long-lived or difficult to realise while its obligations require continued refinancing. If access to funding weakens, management may need to replace maturing liabilities on harder terms, preserve liquidity, dispose of assets, or reduce new lending. Those responses can constrain flexibility and make the next refinancing point more difficult.

That mechanism can become visible before reported action-zone metrics register it. Thresholds concern disclosed levels or deterioration. A funding lens is instead directed at whether the existing balance sheet can be carried through future maturity points. For IL&FS, the 38-month interval is meaningful as a diligence prompt: inspect liability maturity, refinancing dependence, asset liquidity, and the credibility of reported numbers. It is not evidence that another institution will follow the same clock.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. IL&FS was fraud-masked. If public disclosures were distorted, the funding index may have been an incidental early pattern rather than an actionable diagnosis. The absence of a PCA first action-zone entry may reveal the limits of reported data and threshold engineering, rather than a lack of genuine solvency or liquidity pressure.

The validation record also demands restraint. The hazard panel has 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions; 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Leave-one-institution-out AUC was 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic score reached 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic recorded AUC of 0.645 against a gate of 0.65 and failed; its promotion effect is none. Construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote.

Accordingly, the defensible conclusion is not that funding screens identify failures. It is only that disclosed liability strain may warrant earlier forensic scrutiny than a capital-style dashboard alone would prompt.

## What today's board shares

Today’s board is a separate dated screen, not an extension of the IL&FS replay. As of 2026-08-28, it has 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions; 21 stale cases are excluded. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design, not judged low risk.

ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow as of 2025-09-30, aged 11 months, with score 66.0 and market distance-to-default of 1.927. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow as of 2026-03-31, aged 5 months, with score 77.8. These are published screening outputs, not assertions of imminent distress.

The market layer is dated 2026-08-11, not the board date. That is system context, not institution evidence.

## The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if fresh vetted disclosures show that funding-watch institutions do not deteriorate earlier in refinancing capacity, liability structure, or balance-sheet resilience than peers without that signal. articles.headline: Global Trust Bank’s warning appeared before the event—but its limits matter as much as its lead
articles.dek: The replay shows reported capital and asset-quality breaches before Global Trust Bank’s default, while an unscoreable funding lens and a fraud-masked record make the case for escalation, not prediction.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Global Trust Bank using a construction-PIT record. The historical disclosure sequence, current market observations, and current board are different clocks and must not be treated as one signal.*

The narrow thesis is that Global Trust Bank first showed observable stress through reported balance-sheet weakness: capital adequacy and net non-performing assets crossed the replayed action-zone screen before default. The funding lens did not offer a rival early call because it was unscoreable. That is not evidence that funding was sound. It is missing evidence.

The more important qualification is the fraud-masked designation. A filing-period threshold can identify strain in reported data; it cannot verify that reported data describe the underlying institution. Nor should a later market-price signal be read back into a filing replay. And a model derivation is neither of those things: it is a rule constructed from inputs, assumptions and availability conventions. The warning therefore warranted investigation. It did not establish a forecastable path to failure.

## The record before the event

Global Trust Bank’s first replayed action-zone entry was at the period ending 2002-03-31, identified as FY2002. The breached measures were CRAR and NNPA. The record assigns a knowledge-time proxy of 2002-05-30 and a lead of 25 months to the 2004-07-24 default date.

That sequence is a filing-period signal, not proof of what supervisors knew privately or what the balance sheet economically contained. The PCA lens is a public-disclosure replay of the RBI’s own PCA/SAF tripwires. Its summary covers 15 failed institutions; 5 entered the action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. Global Trust Bank’s lead is therefore an observation inside a small historical set, not a timetable that can be exported to another institution.

The historical construction uses an explicit publication clock where available; otherwise it applies period end plus 60 days. That availability convention is deliberately conservative relative to simply assuming contemporaneous knowledge, but it remains a proxy. The dossier says lead times are optimistic and the record lacks a bitemporal input contract. Those limits matter before any apparent early warning is called predictive. The underlying constraints are set out in the [Failure Radar validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation).

## What the lenses saw

The primary balance-sheet lens saw CRAR and NNPA breaches. This is the core filing-period observation: reported capital capacity and reported asset quality simultaneously met the action-zone conditions. It supports a concern that disclosed loss-absorption capacity could be under pressure if asset-quality deterioration required recognition. It does not reveal unreported exposures, establish causation, or reconstruct management decisions.

The funding lens saw no scoreable series. Global Trust Bank has no first funding signal and no funding lead time in the record. Across the failed-institution funding summary, liability disclosures exist for 10 of 15 institutions, and the funding signal fired first for 4. The lens can only assess institutions that disclose a liability series. An unscoreable result is consequently an observation boundary, not an all-clear.

The fraud-masked tag supplies a third, distinct category of evidence. It is not a contemporaneous market-price signal and not a ratio crossing. It states the key failure mode: filings later shown falsified can look compliant, or only partly impaired, to a threshold engine. The forensic screen owns that problem. The balance-sheet screen may still have found a useful symptom, but it could not authenticate the numbers it received.

## Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because it converted diffuse concern into an auditable escalation condition. A CRAR and NNPA breach gave an analyst a reason to ask whether reported capital could absorb further recognition of asset-quality weakness, whether disclosures were sufficiently reliable, and whether liabilities required separate investigation.

That is a weaker and more defensible claim than saying the screen predicted default. The recorded 25-month lead created time for diligence, not a countdown. It also did not make funding stress visible: the relevant series was unavailable to the lens. And fraud masking means even the observed balance-sheet sequence may understate, distort, or incompletely represent the condition it appears to measure.

India’s broader evidence should be read with the same restraint. The construction-PIT diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. Yet it is explicitly not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and not supported by a bitemporal input contract. The [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) labels it a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT diagnostic, rather than a prospective performance record.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat any stronger version of this thesis. Global Trust Bank was fraud-masked. If the disclosed record was unreliable, CRAR and NNPA breaches may be imperfect symptoms rather than a clean diagnosis of the actual balance sheet. The replay establishes ordering in available public data, not the full economic chronology of the institution’s distress.

The validation sample also does not justify broad certainty. Only 5 of 15 failed institutions entered the PCA action zone first. The funding lens cannot corroborate or challenge this case because Global Trust Bank was unscoreable. A missing liability series leaves a meaningful part of the pressure chain unobserved.

Nor can a construction-PIT result become a current investment claim by repetition. The proxy clock, lack of bitemporal inputs, and optimistic lead-time warning prevent that move. The strongest warranted conclusion is only that reported CRAR and NNPA deterioration supplied a legitimate trigger for deeper scrutiny before the event. It was insufficient to infer default, dismiss funding risk, or overcome a forensic-data problem.

## What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this historical replay. As of 2026-08-28, it contains 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green institutions, while excluding 21 stale cases by design. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with a 2025-03-31 as-of date and age of 17 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, with a 2025-09-30 as-of date, age of 11 months, and market distance-to-default of 1.927. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, with a 2026-03-31 as-of date and age of 5 months.

Those are current board classifications, not extensions of the Global Trust Bank evidence. The [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) uses one fresh vetted public dossier per institution and does not score absent institutions from memory. Its market layer is dated 2026-08-11 and uses Yahoo Finance daily auto-adjusted closes. That is a market-price signal with its own date, distinct from a filing date and distinct again from a model-derived tier.

The board’s conformal alarm is retained as a diagnostic, but its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. A tier is a published rule over published components, not a credit rating or a failure forecast.

## The next falsifiable test

The thesis would weaken if fresh, vetted disclosures showed that institutions flagged by reported capital, asset-quality, or market-distance conditions did not sustain deterioration while comparable unflagged institutions did. It would weaken further if prospectively timestamped disclosure records failed to preserve the observed order between warning and later stress.

For this replay specifically, the claim would be challenged if a forensic review found that the CRAR and NNPA crossings had no durable relationship to balance-sheet pressure once reliable information was available. Conversely, a prospective record in which independently verified deterioration precedes weaker resilience would support the narrower use of these screens as escalation tools. Neither result follows automatically from a historical replay.

## Follow the pressure chain

The useful chain is deliberately incomplete: reported asset-quality and capital pressure; lower apparent capacity to absorb losses; deeper verification of the reported balance sheet; and, where disclosed, separate examination of liabilities, market repricing, and forensic indicators. The chain stops at missing evidence. Global Trust Bank’s funding series was unscoreable, and fraud masking means ratio analysis cannot close the gap.

A system read does not prove an institution-level failure path, and a market-liquidity observation does not validate a filing-period ratio.

This historical replay is not current news and not a forecast.

Altico’s record supports a narrow answer to the desk question. The balance sheet that should have been examined first was its funding structure: commercial-paper reliance created exposure to a rollover freeze. That is not the same as saying a market had priced default, that a regulatory action-zone measure had deteriorated, or that a model had produced a reliable probability of failure.

The relevant filing-period observation is for **2017-03-31**: a funding index of **23.7**, a **stable** band, and a flag for commercial-paper reliance of **29%** with rollover-freeze exposure. The stated knowledge-time proxy is **2017-05-30**. Altico defaulted on **2019-09-12**; the replay records a funding lead of **27 months**. The funding index nevertheless sat in the **stable** band at **23.7**.

That combination should restrain, rather than inflate, the conclusion. The filing-period signal was a disclosed funding flag. It was not an escalating funding-band alarm. Nor does the record supply a market-price signal for Altico. A market signal would be a price-based observation, such as the board’s market distance-to-default measure for names where that layer is available; none is provided for this Altico replay.

The PCA record also cannot be made to say more than it says. Altico has no first action-zone date and no PCA lead-month figure. Missing timing is not evidence that a PCA-style threshold found calm, and it is not evidence that such a threshold would necessarily have warned later. It means the record cannot rank PCA against the funding lens for Altico. The supportable finding is limited to the disclosed, scoreable funding lens.

Readers can inspect the historical framing through [Altico’s replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/altico/) and the [failure-radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board). The funding lens saw a filing-period vulnerability: commercial-paper reliance and associated rollover-freeze exposure. It recorded the first signal at **2017-03-31**, assigned the **stable** band, and uses **2017-05-30** as the knowledge-time proxy. Those are distinct fields, and they matter. Period end identifies when the reported condition belongs; the knowledge-time proxy approximates when it may have become available; the band summarizes the lens; the flag identifies the specific concern.

The PCA lens did not provide a usable first-action-zone timestamp. Therefore this article does not claim that funding beat PCA in a direct, complete horse race. The warning mattered because it described a concrete liability-side exposure before the default date. Commercial paper must be refinanced. But plausibility is not proof of a complete causal history. The evidence does not provide a contemporaneous Altico market-price series, an observed rollover refusal, or a dated PCA breach. It also does not permit the **stable** band to be rewritten as measured acute distress. The responsible reading is that a stable composite band coexisted with a specific funding flag, and that the flag was the first recorded signal in the replay.

The counter-case can defeat any stronger thesis. Commercial-paper reliance of **29%** does not itself demonstrate imminent failure. Altico’s funding index was **23.7** and classified as **stable**. Where an explicit publication clock is absent, availability uses period end plus **60 days**. The dossier states plainly that lead times are optimistic, that there is no bitemporal input contract, and that the work is neither validated-backtest eligible nor real-money eligible.

## What today's board shares

The current board is as of **2026-08-27**; its market layer is as of **2026-08-11**. These are not Altico dates and must not be blended with the replay. The board has **0** red, **1** orange, **3** yellow and **15** green institutions, while **21** stale cases are excluded. Nothing older than **24 months** is presented as current.

The useful shared discipline is to distinguish filing as-of dates, availability dates and market-price dates. The [market-evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) describes the diagnostic context; it does not fill Altico’s missing market signal.

That distinction matters because hindsight can turn an early ratio into an apparently complete explanation. This dossier supports only the opening link: a fragile funding classification and a stated leverage flag. It does not establish the subsequent pressure chain.

articles.headline: Nedungadi Bank’s capital breach preceded the event. The harder question is what that warning could—and could not—establish.

*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines information associated with Nedungadi Bank before its default date, rather than asserting that similar mechanisms must produce the same outcome elsewhere. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome.*

Nedungadi Bank is a useful stress case precisely because the record is incomplete. The replay records a CRAR breach that put the bank into an RBI action zone at FY1999. Its default date is later. That sequence makes capital a serious investigative signal, but it does not establish that capital caused the outcome, that funding was sound, or that an observer could have known every relevant fact in real time.

The essential distinction is temporal. A filing-period signal describes a reported condition at a period end. The replay translates that into an availability estimate using an explicit publication clock when present, or a filing-lag proxy when it is not. A market-price signal is a separate repricing measure, available only where market data exist and dated on its own clock. A model derivation combines published components under stated rules; it is neither a filing nor a market quote. The first recorded action-zone observation for Nedungadi Bank is FY1999, with period end `1999-03-31`, status `threshold_1`, and CRAR listed as the breach. The replay uses `1999-05-30` as its knowledge-time proxy. The default date is `2002-11-02`, and the reported lead is `41` months. The supplied record does not mark the institution fraud-masked.

That is a material sequence, not a completed causal narrative. It says that a supervisory tripwire was publicly reconstructable before the event under the replay’s timing convention. It does not show what management knew, what creditors did, whether a recapitalisation route existed, or whether other pressures were more decisive.

The funding lens supplies no compensating answer. Nedungadi is explicitly unscoreable for funding, with no first signal and no funding lead time. Missing liability disclosure is an information boundary, not evidence that liabilities were stable. In the failed-institution funding summary, `10` of `15` had liability disclosures and `4` had a funding signal fire first; median lead was `38` months. The capital-first observation cannot therefore be converted into a finding that the bank’s funding position was benign.

An action-zone breach mattered because it identified a disclosed supervisory threshold crossing before the event. That is enough to justify a fuller inquiry into the balance sheet. It is not enough to declare a failure path inevitable.

The `41`-month lead is ambiguous in both directions. It may show that the action-zone lens surfaced an issue well before default. It also leaves room for recovery, changed conditions, measurement error, interventions, and developments not captured by this replay. Long lead time is not automatically stronger proof; it increases the importance of asking whether later evidence confirmed or contradicted the early signal.

The proper interpretation is conditional: a CRAR breach can be the first observable link in a pressure chain. Whether it became decisive would require evidence on losses, funding, disclosure quality, supervisory constraints, and market repricing at their respective availability times. The dossier does not supply that complete chain for Nedungadi.

The counter-case can defeat any claim that Nedungadi proves a general capital-first thesis. The model evidence is also not a rescue. The hazard panel has `205` rows, `9` events, and `27` institutions; `179` censored or unusable rows were excluded. articles.headline: Utkarsh is the orange balance-sheet watch, but the evidence is aging
articles.dek: Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is the sole orange name on the current LiquiLens Failure Radar. That status rests on an old filing-period asset-quality signal, not on a market verdict, a funding event, or a prediction of failure.
articles.body_markdown:
## The finding

Among institutions represented by fresh-enough vetted public dossiers on the current LiquiLens screen, Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is the clearest balance-sheet pressure watch. This is deliberately narrower than a claim that the bank will fail, has an imminent liquidity problem, or is currently weaker than every institution outside the screen.

The orange designation rests on a filing-period signal. The subject dossier is dated **2025-03-31** and records GNPA of **9.4%**. Its corpus-monitoring probability measure is **0.0031**, compared with **0.0016** for FY2024. The published hazard basis names GNPA of **9.4%**. Under the radar rule, orange can result from a probability level at or above **1.00%**, deterioration from at least **0.25%**, or market distance to default below **1**. Utkarsh has no reported market distance-to-default calculation.

Time is the crucial qualification. The dossier's knowledge-time proxy is **2025-05-30**, while the article date is **2026-08-21**; subject evidence is **17** months old. The [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) shows no red names, one orange name, three yellow names, and **15** green names. But it is a published rule applied to vetted dossiers, not a census of every institution's current condition.

This is a corpus monitoring probability, not a credit rating. The conditional conclusion is simply that, if the reported deterioration endured after the filing period, Utkarsh's credit losses, earnings, and capital would warrant close monitoring within this disclosed universe.

## The mechanism

The proposed pressure chain begins with impaired assets, not a claim about a deposit run. GNPA of **9.4%** is the disclosed datum behind the watch. If credit quality remained impaired, losses could constrain earnings; weaker earnings could limit retained capital; and less capital capacity could make a later funding or confidence shock more consequential.

That chain is a model derivation, not an observed sequence in current Utkarsh data. The dossier does not say that every link has occurred. It records a change in a model measure and an orange rule outcome. The measure also provides **24**-month values, but these are model outputs, not traded prices of default protection and not observed failure frequencies.

Capital is the important offset in the same filing. CRAR is **20.93**, with **5.93** percentage points of headroom over the **15.0** licensing CRAR floor. Small finance banks are outside the **2021** bank-PCA framework, so this is not an RBI action-zone breach. The relevant tension is between a reported capital cushion at a point in time and an asset-quality path that might consume it if it persisted. Neither observation cancels the other.

## What the filings say

The filing record supports three direct statements: GNPA was **9.4%**; CRAR was **20.93**; and the capital figure exceeded the **15.0** floor. It does not support a PCA-breach claim, because PCA is marked not applicable. It does not establish funding stress, because the funding lens is not scored. It does not provide the liability stack needed to set a market default barrier.

The dossier uses an explicit publication clock when available and otherwise applies period end plus **60** days. Its historical status is period-end-proxy construction-PIT. The conservative lag reduces quarter-end look-ahead, but cannot recreate overwritten amendments or a complete archive of public availability and revisions. The dossier explicitly says lead times are optimistic.

That limitation makes the filing signal useful but bounded. It describes what the disclosed FY2025 record showed, not what occurred during the following **17** months. The stale date cannot be treated as evidence of calm. Equally, an old adverse asset-quality datum cannot be treated as proof of present distress.

## What the market says

The market does not independently confirm the Utkarsh case. A market layer is available as of **2026-08-11** and includes Utkarsh, but market distance to default is not computed because no disclosed liability stack can set a default barrier. That is missing measurement, not a favourable market-price signal.

Peer comparisons do not fill this gap. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow with market distance to default of **1.927**. IndusInd Bank is yellow with **2.925**. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow without a reported market value. None supplies Utkarsh's missing liability structure or updates its filing. The relevant coverage is available through the [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets).

System and exit conditions require separate treatment. Seiche addresses **system dollar-funding capacity**. Its composite is **45.0**, labelled STRAIN, while its editorial notes that the calendar carries the strain call and overnight-cash pricing still says abundance. This is guarded context, not a verdict on an Indian small finance bank; see the [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview). Undertow addresses **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**. Its IG segment is NORMAL, while several other segments are PARTIAL, on the [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json). Neither product measures Utkarsh solvency.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. Utkarsh reported material CRAR headroom over its licensing floor. No PCA breach is recorded, no forensic indicator fired, and no funding flag fired. Its probability level is below the **1.00%** level threshold in the tier rule. Orange is not red.

More decisively, the adverse evidence is old. A newer vetted filing could show that GNPA stabilised or improved, capital remained resilient, and the modelled deterioration did not persist. If so, describing Utkarsh as the first balance sheet likely to feel stress would confuse a past filing-period warning with current financial condition.

Dark funding evidence does not defeat this counter-case. “Not scored” is neither proof of sound funding nor proof of strain. Similarly, missing market distance to default is neither market comfort nor market confirmation. Capital and unknown subsequent performance could outweigh the old asset-quality signal.

## The evidence that is dark

Several potentially decisive lenses are unavailable. Deposit-run analysis is dark because there are no consecutive deposit disclosures. Wholesale reliance, CD strain, and LCR headroom are also dark. Funding has no index, band, or basis. The forensic screen is ineligible. The market measure cannot be calculated without a disclosed liability stack.

These gaps preserve the difference between absence of evidence and evidence of absence. The radar excludes **21** stale institutions. Its method allows one row per institution with a vetted public dossier and says institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design: nothing is scored from memory. The [US NDFI watch](https://api.liquilens.in/api/us-radar/ndfi) cannot repair those missing Utkarsh disclosures or serve as evidence about Utkarsh.

## What would change the call

A fresh eligible disclosure would weaken the case if it showed stabilising or improved credit quality, resilient CRAR, and newly disclosed funding or liability information without adverse flags. It would strengthen the case if it showed further asset-quality deterioration, capital erosion toward the **15.0** floor, a funding warning, a forensic indicator, or enough liability data to calculate an adverse market signal.

The falsification test is direct: a new vetted dossier must establish whether the FY2025 deterioration persisted. If subsequent disclosure shows stabilisation and maintained capital, the thesis fails on its own terms. A monitoring signal is not entitled to survive contrary evidence.

## Follow the pressure chain

Follow separate lenses rather than a headline tier. Begin with the [LiquiLens Failure Radar](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), then inspect the [validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation). LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity**. Undertow covers **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**. These are complementary research boundaries, not interchangeable proof.

For methodology and dossier context, consult the [LiquiLens research archive](https://liquilens.in/research/) and the [replay archive](https://liquilens.in/replay/). This framework provides monitoring, not a trade instruction.

## Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the supplied dossier, the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), the [validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), the market evidence index, Seiche, and Undertow. Historical evidence is construction-PIT and **not validated-backtest eligible**. It is also **not real-money eligible** and lacks a complete bitemporal input contract.

The hazard record has **205** rows, **9** events, and **27** institutions; **179** censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its temporal AUC is **0.645** against a **0.65** gate and did not pass. The conformal diagnostic is closed pending revalidation, its wiring is suspended, and it has no score or tier authority. Filings later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that limitation. These boundaries support monitoring an old filing signal, not forecasting Utkarsh's failure.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

articles.headline: ESAF’s stress signal is not funding flight. It is a narrowing margin for error.
articles.dek: ESAF Small Finance Bank is a yellow-screen priority because an asset-quality burden and a stale market repricing signal can interact before a visible funding break. The available deposit signal is stable, while key liquidity evidence remains dark.

## The finding

ESAF Small Finance Bank is the balance sheet in this screen most likely to merit early scrutiny if financial stress develops. That is not the same as saying that it will fail first, that it is already in a funding event, or that its deposits are running. The available evidence supports a narrower proposition: reported asset-quality pressure and a market-derived fragility signal could leave the institution more exposed to a further adverse turn before a clean funding signal makes that turn obvious.

The filing snapshot is dated **2025-09-30**, in **FY26Q2**, and is **11** months old at publication. The market layer is dated **2026-08-11**, is also marked stale, and the article date is **2026-08-20**. Those clocks cannot be merged into a claim about one contemporaneous condition.

LiquiLens assigns ESAF a yellow tier and a score of **66.0**. Yellow is a published screen, not a credit rating, insolvency finding, or investment instruction. ESAF’s recorded fired signal is market distance-to-default below **2**. The model’s corpus-monitoring **12**-month probability is **0.0042**, from **0.0034** in FY25Q2. Its stated scope is “corpus monitoring probability not credit rating.”

## The mechanism

The filing-period mechanism begins with gross non-performing assets. ESAF’s hazard record identifies GNPA of **8.5%** as its basis. A larger impaired-loan stock can demand greater loss absorption if credit performance deteriorates further. That can narrow a bank’s capacity to absorb subsequent shocks, and a thinner perceived cushion can amplify market sensitivity.

But this is a causal chain to monitor, not proof that every link has occurred. The dossier does not provide a loss forecast, a current capital-ratio assessment, wholesale-funding pricing, or liquidity-coverage headroom. Small finance banks are outside the cited **2021** bank-PCA framework. CRAR is not assessed, and no headroom is supplied against the stated **15%** licensing CRAR floor.

The distinction matters. GNPA is a filing-period signal. The probability movement is a model derivation from the monitoring corpus. Neither is a live market price, and neither demonstrates an imminent funding rupture.

## What the filings say

The filings supply an uncomfortable but incomplete combination: GNPA of **8.5%** at the period end, alongside a stable funding classification. The funding lens records the worst deposit quarter-on-quarter change as positive **5.3%**, gives the funding index as **0.0**, and records no funding flags.

That is why the case is not a deposit-run narrative. Stable deposits can coexist with asset-quality pressure; equally, positive deposit growth does not establish durable liquidity resilience. Wholesale reliance, certificate-of-deposit strain, and liquidity-coverage headroom are explicitly dark lenses.

The forensics screen was eligible and did not fire. Its correct interpretation is narrow: the supplied forensic indicators did not fire. It does not certify the accounts or make missing liquidity data reassuring.

The wider radar shows **0** red institutions, **1** orange, **3** yellow, and **15** green. ESAF’s peer percentile is **100** in a cohort of **4**, a comparison too small to become a broad sector verdict. The radar also excludes **21** stale cases. The market signal is sharper in form and weaker in interpretation than the filings. ESAF’s naive Bharath-Shumway distance-to-default is **1.927**, producing the yellow trigger. The associated Merton-form probability is **0.02696**. The dossier is explicit: this is a repricing and ranking signal, not a probability calibrated to Indian failure frequencies.

Inputs include market capitalisation of Rs **2,056** cr, equity volatility of **42.9%** using **252**-day realised volatility, prior-**1**-year return of positive **27.7%**, and a Rs **23,276** cr barrier from FY25Q4 disclosures. The barrier is slightly understated because other liabilities are not in the schema. Thus the signal cannot be read as a complete balance-sheet valuation, much less a resolution forecast.

The [market evidence feed](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) identifies Yahoo Finance daily auto-adjusted closes as its source. It is useful for detecting market repricing, but it is stale here and does not replace fresher disclosures.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. Deposits were growing in the available quarter, the funding band is stable, the funding index is **0.0**, and no forensic indicator fired. The corpus-monitoring probability is below the radar’s **1.00%** level threshold. Meanwhile, the market trigger rests on a naive model with an incomplete barrier and a stale observation.

A second restraint comes from system context. Seiche describes a guarded STRAIN reading of **45.3**, where calendar structure carries the call while the price of overnight cash still indicates abundance. Its note says slow-moving or modelled structure leads while current plumbing has not broadly confirmed it. That is not direct evidence about ESAF, and it argues against declaring a general liquidity shock. See [Seiche’s overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview).

On this view, ESAF is not the institution certain to feel stress first. It is simply the current yellow-screen case whose live-looking market signal most clearly deserves to be tested against new filings.

## The evidence that is dark

Several decisive facts are missing: wholesale reliance, certificate-of-deposit strain, liquidity-coverage headroom, CRAR headroom, and other liabilities used in a complete market-model barrier. The filing snapshot is old and the market observation is stale.

These blanks are not evidence of calm. Nor does a non-fired forensic screen rule out later-discovered falsification. The validation material notes that threshold engines can show compliance where filings are later shown false. Missing data therefore weakens both a bullish dismissal and a bearish certainty.

## What would change the call

The case would weaken if fresher vetted disclosures showed improving asset quality, demonstrated capital and liquidity headroom, and a refreshed distance-to-default above **2**. It would also weaken if the market signal ceased to be ESAF’s sole fired signal.

The case would strengthen if new disclosures showed worsening asset quality, a funding flag emerged, or a refreshed market reading remained below **2**. The conformal alarm should not settle the question: it is CLOSED_REVALIDATION_REQUIRED, its wiring is suspended, and it has no tier authority.

## Follow the pressure chain

Keep product boundaries separate. LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**; its [articles](https://liquilens.in/articles/), [investigations](https://liquilens.in/investigations/), and [replay archive](https://liquilens.in/replay/) address that institutional chain.

Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity**, not ESAF’s individual balance sheet. Undertow covers **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**. Its board classifies IG as NORMAL while other segments are PARTIAL, with observations from **2026-06-30** through **2026-08-20**. That is a coverage description, not an ESAF conclusion. Consult [Undertow’s board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) and [Undertow articles](https://liquilens-undertow.com/articles/).

## Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the dossier and permitted links only. The radar is one row per institution with a fresh vetted public dossier; nothing older than **24** months is presented as current. Historical evidence is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT: an explicit publication clock is used when available, otherwise period end plus a conservative **60**-day filing proxy. Historical validation is diagnostic only. The temporal hazard test reports AUC of **0.645** against a **0.65** gate and does not pass. Construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote. Further method material is available through [LiquiLens research](https://liquilens.in/research/) and the [LiquiLens pilot](https://liquilens.in/pilot/).

The conclusion remains deliberately conditional: ESAF merits first scrutiny because filing-period asset-quality pressure and a stale market-price signal could interact before visible funding stress. The evidence does not establish that funding stress is under way. Research and market data, not investment advice.

articles.headline: Religare Finvest replay: a funding watch came before default, but fraud limits what it can prove
articles.dek: The historical record places a disclosed-liability warning ahead of Religare Finvest’s default. It does not show that a threshold screen detected fraud, established causation, or supplied a tradeable forecast.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Religare Finvest defaulted on 2018-01-18. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome.*

Religare Finvest is a test of a deliberately narrow proposition: which visible balance-sheet channel registered pressure first? The recorded answer is funding. The scoreable liability lens entered its watch band at the 2016-03-31 period end, with an index of 44.3, and the replay assigns a 19-month lead to default. But this is also a fraud-masked case. That designation is not a footnote: it prevents the stronger claim that the screen saw the condition that caused failure.

The distinction is threefold. The funding reading is a filing-period signal: a measure drawn from disclosed balance-sheet information at a reported period end. Its knowledge-time proxy is 2016-05-30, using the stated 60-day convention. It is not a market-price signal, and it is not a model derivation of a calibrated failure probability. The lead is therefore a historical construction-PIT observation, not proof that an investor could have acted on it at that time.

## The record before the event

Religare Finvest is classified as an NBFC. Its funding record is scoreable; the first signal is recorded at the 2016-03-31 period end, in the watch band, with no listed flags. Under the availability convention, the information is treated as knowable on 2016-05-30. The event date is 2018-01-18.

The public-action-zone replay supplies no competing early signal: first action zone and lead months are both absent. That is not evidence that the institution was safe. It means only that the available replay did not establish an action-zone entry before default.

The [Religare Finvest replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/religare-finvest/) should thus be read separately from the current [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board). One is a reconstruction of a failed institution; the other is a current screened universe. Neither converts a missing disclosure, an absent tripwire, or a non-fired flag into evidence of calm.

## What the lenses saw

The funding lens provides the earliest recorded alert. It speaks to disclosed liability conditions and the possibility that refinancing flexibility was narrowing. That is a balance-sheet mechanism, not a verified account of every transaction or decision at Religare Finvest.

The action-zone lens asks a different question: whether public disclosures crossed replayed RBI PCA or SAF tripwires. Across the historical summary, 15 failed institutions are covered, 5 entered the action zone first, and median lead is 41 months. The funding summary also covers 15 failed institutions, but liability disclosures exist for only 10; funding fired first for 4, with median lead of 38 months. Those figures establish neither a universal ordering nor a production forecasting edge.

The market layer is different again. Its Merton PD is a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. Market distance-to-default can inform a current board classification, but it cannot be retrofitted into this filing-period observation. The [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) and the replay answer adjacent, not identical, questions.

## Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because liabilities can transmit stress into lending capacity before a public action-zone measure is recorded. A lender facing funding pressure may have less flexibility in refinancing or balance-sheet choices. That can make later asset, capital, or governance weaknesses harder to absorb.
